title: Files and I/O
intro: Reading and writing files lives in `std::fs` (whole files at once) and `std::io` (streams, buffers, line by line). Almost every call that touches the disk returns an `io::Result`, and `?` passes the error up to the caller.

coming_from.go: `fs::write` is `os.WriteFile`, and `fs::read_to_string` is `os.ReadFile` plus `string()` plus a UTF-8 check that can fail. `BufReader::lines()` takes the place of `bufio.Scanner`, and `?` replaces each `if err != nil`. A `File` closes at the end of its scope, but unlike `f.Close()` that cannot return an error.
coming_from.kotlin: `fs::write` and `fs::read_to_string` are `writeText` and `readText`. Failures come back as `io::Result` instead of exceptions, and a file closes when it goes out of scope, as if every use were wrapped in `use { }`, except that a failed close is not reported.
coming_from.python: `fs::read_to_string` is `path.read_text()` and `fs::write` is `path.write_text()`. A file closes when its variable goes out of scope, like the end of a `with` block, and errors come back as a `Result` instead of a raised `OSError`. Bad UTF-8 is an `io::Error` too, not a `UnicodeDecodeError`.
coming_from.typescript: `std::fs` is like the `*Sync` functions in `node:fs`: plain blocking calls, and reading line by line needs no `async`. Errors come back as a `Result`, and `e.kind()` plays the role of `err.code`.
coming_from.java: `fs::write` and `fs::read_to_string` are `Files.writeString` and `Files.readString`, and a call that can fail returns `io::Result` instead of throwing `IOException`. Files close when they go out of scope, like try-with-resources but automatic, except that a failed close is not reported. You do need `use std::io::Read` to get methods like `read_to_string` on a `File`.
coming_from.csharp: `fs::write` and `fs::read_to_string` are `File.WriteAllText` and `File.ReadAllText`, but errors come back as `io::Result` for `?`, not as exceptions. A `File` closes when it goes out of scope, like `using` without the keyword (and without an exception from a failed close), and trait methods like `read_to_string` need a `use std::io::Read`.
coming_from.c: `File` is closer to a file descriptor than to a `FILE *`: it has no buffer (`BufReader` and `BufWriter` add one), and it closes itself at the end of its scope, so there's no `fclose` to forget. A failing call returns a `Result` with the error kind inside, instead of `NULL` plus `errno`.
coming_from.cpp: `File` is RAII like `std::fstream`, closed at the end of its scope, but it has no buffer where an `fstream` has one. Every read and write returns an `io::Result` that you must handle, instead of a stream fail bit that's easy to ignore.

notes: `fs::write`, `fs::read_to_string` and `fs::read` (bytes) are the one-liners. Reach for `File` plus `BufReader` or `BufWriter` when the file is big or you want it line by line.

`reader.lines()` gives you `Result<String>` items, not plain Strings. That's why there's a `let line = line?;` inside the loop. Each read can fail, and you get that error on the line where it happened. Ignoring a `Result` draws a compiler warning.

A `File` has no buffer of its own: `lines()` needs a `BufReader`, and many small writes want a `BufWriter`. Dropping a `File` closes it but cannot report a failed close, so call `sync_all` or `flush` where you must know.

Paths are their own type, `Path` (borrowed) and `PathBuf` (owned), like `&str` and `String`. File names on Linux don't have to be valid UTF-8, so a path isn't just a string. `.join()` is `filepath.Join`, except that an absolute second part replaces the first.

`fs::write(&path, ...)` borrows the path. Functions like this take `impl AsRef<Path>`, which means "anything that can be read as a path": a `&str`, a `String`, a `PathBuf`. [Reading signatures](/learn/reading-signatures/) explains that bound.

Writing with `writeln!` needs `use std::io::Write`, and `.lines()` needs `use std::io::BufRead`. Those methods come from traits, and a trait has to be imported before its methods show up. That's the gotcha below.

gotcha.title: Calling a method that's "right there" on a File
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Java, Python, TypeScript and C# a method belongs to its type: if the file has `Read`, you can call it anywhere you have a file. Nothing else to import.
gotcha.rust_sees: `read_to_string` isn't a method of `File` itself. It comes from the `Read` trait, and trait methods only exist where the trait is imported with `use`.
gotcha.why: Many std types get most of their methods from traits: `Read`, `Write`, `BufRead`, `Iterator`, `FromStr`. Rust only looks at traits you've brought into scope, so two crates can add methods with the same name without clashing. The compiler error tells you exactly which `use` line to add. Copy it and move on.

go.says: Go runs this and prints hello. `Read` is a method on the file itself, so there is nothing extra to import.
go.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	path := filepath.Join(os.TempDir(), "rbc-hello.txt")
	os.WriteFile(path, []byte("hello"), 0o644)

	f, _ := os.Open(path)
	buf := make([]byte, 64)
	n, _ := f.Read(buf)
	fmt.Println(string(buf[:n]))
	f.Close()
	os.Remove(path)
}

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints hello, because `reader()` and `readText()` come from `kotlin.io`, which is imported by default. Kotlin has the Rust rule too: the same `readText()` on a `java.nio.file.Path` does not compile until you add `import kotlin.io.path.readText`.

python.says: Python prints hello. `read` is a method of the file object itself, so there is nothing extra to import before you can call it.
python.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "rbc-hello.txt"
path.write_text("hello")

with open(path) as f:
    text = f.read()
print(text)
path.unlink()

typescript.says: Prints hello. Node's file functions are plain functions in the `fs` module, so once it's imported every one of them is there.

java.says: In Java a method belongs to its class, so `readAllBytes` is right there on the stream with no extra import, and this prints hello.

csharp.says: `ReadToEnd` is a method of StreamReader itself, so it's there with no extra `using`, and this prints hello. Extension methods like LINQ's do need a `using`, but the project's implicit usings already bring in the common ones.

c.says: C has a cousin of this mistake: forget `#include <string.h>` and GCC 14 refuses `strcspn` and `strlen`, and even suggests the header, much like rustc suggests `use std::io::Read`.

cpp.says: C++ refuses this too: without `#include <fstream>`, `std::ofstream` and `std::ifstream` are only declared, so g++ calls them incomplete types. For `std::ifstream` it also names the header to add, `<fstream>`.

python.code:
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

path = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "rbc-notes.txt"

# write a whole file at once (creates it, or empties it first)
path.write_text("milk\neggs\n")

# open for appending and add a line
with open(path, "a") as f:
    f.write("bread\n")

# read the whole file into one str
text = path.read_text()
print(f"{len(text)} chars")

# read line by line, without loading the whole file
with open(path) as f:  # `with` closes the file at the end of the block
    for i, line in enumerate(f, start=1):
        print(f"{i}: {line.rstrip()}")

print(f"file name: {path.name!r}")

# a missing file raises an exception you can catch
try:
    Path("/no/such/file.txt").read_text()
except FileNotFoundError as e:
    print(f"error: {e.strerror} (errno {e.errno})")

path.unlink()

files.py.code:
import os
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

try:
    Path("/no/such/file.txt").read_text()
except OSError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ":", e)

path = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "lr-fio-py.txt"
path.write_bytes(b"bad \xff here\n")
try:
    path.read_text()
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print(type(e).__name__ + ":", e, "| an OSError:", isinstance(e, OSError))

# text mode translates line endings on the way in; Rust's read_to_string does not
path.write_bytes(b"one\r\ntwo\r\n")
with open(path, "rb") as f:
    print("bytes:", f.read())
with open(path) as f:
    print("for line in f:", list(f))  # each line keeps its \n
with open(path, newline="") as f:
    print("newline='':", repr(f.read()))
print("suffix of a.tar.gz:", Path("a.tar.gz").suffix)  # Rust's extension() has no dot


def write_calls():
    with open("/proc/self/io") as f:
        return int(next(l for l in f if l.startswith("syscw:")).split()[1])


# open() buffers; a Rust File does not
with open(path, "w") as f:
    before = write_calls()
    for i in range(1000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n")
    during = write_calls() - before
print("1000 f.write calls:", during, "write calls before close,", write_calls() - before, "after")
os.remove(path)

print("Path('/data') / '/etc/hosts':", Path("/data") / "/etc/hosts")
